strengths: Sound technical framework: Multimodal flow formulation with decoupled time variables correctly combines CTMC for discrete atoms and ODE for continuous structures, with appropriate use of geodesic flows on the torus for periodicity preservation

Novel domain-specific innovations: Composition- and symmetry-aware atom ordering by electronegativity and Wyckoff position is principled; hierarchical permutation augmentation reduces search space by >11 orders of magnitude and provides strong inductive bias
Superior symmetry preservation: MCFlow better captures space group and Wyckoff position distributions compared to baselines (Figure 4), avoiding mode collapse toward low-symmetry P1 group
Better generalization to larger unit cells: Shows meaningful improvements on MPTS-52 (27.16% MR vs. CrystalFlow 22.71%), suggesting scalability advantage despite acknowledged limitations
Comprehensive evaluation across multiple tasks and benchmarks: CSP, DNG, and ATG on MP-20 and MPTS-52 with detailed ablations (Table 4) and scaling analysis (Figure 8)
Excellent reproducibility: Complete specification of model architectures, training hyperparameters, inference settings, and detailed algorithms; enables reproduction by others
Superior sampling efficiency: MCFlow saturates earlier than baselines in CSP match rate (Figure 3), indicating efficient use of integration steps
Clear presentation with effective visualizations: Figure 1 communicates any-to-any modality concept clearly; Figure 2 effectively illustrates atom ordering strategy
weaknesses: Modest performance gains on standard MP-20 benchmark: Single-sample CSP achieves 64.08% MR (MCFlow-L), underperforming some baselines; multi-sample performance (76.08%) lags CrystalFlow (78.34%), undermining claims of competitive performance on the primary benchmark

Acknowledged but unaddressed scalability limitations: Explicitly states 'challenges remain in scaling to larger unit cells' but only evaluates up to 52 atoms; practical materials discovery often requires larger structures
Low novelty metrics for de novo generation: S.U.N. rates of 16.0% (MCFlow-L) indicate most generated structures fail combined stability+uniqueness+novelty criterion, limiting real-world applicability

Insufficient justification for key design choices: Independent coupling assumption in Eq. 1 lacks ablation study; loss weight choices (0.5/2.0/1.0/1.0) not justified; noisy guidance appears ad-hoc and only applied to single-sample generation
Missing computational cost analysis: No comparison of training/inference efficiency vs. baselines; unclear if 2-4 day training is competitive

Incomplete explanation of Wyckoff position determination during CSP: At inference time when structure is unknown, the mechanism for determining atom positions without Wyckoff information needs clarification beyond 'soft inductive bias'

Permutation robustness claims lack direct validation: Paper claims hierarchical augmentation promotes 'robustness to symmetry-preserving permutations' but provides no direct experimental test of this property
Limited failure mode analysis: Insufficient discussion of when/why MCFlow underperforms baselines, limiting understanding of method limitations
Thermodynamic stability evaluation uncertainty: S.U.N./MS.U.N. metrics rely on CHGNet relaxation with varying convergence rates (99.73% vs. 60.79% for baselines), introducing experimental confounds
Incomplete experimental ablations: Loss weight sensitivity analysis missing; no study of flow time clipping threshold (0.9); unclear impact of noisy guidance disabling in 20-sample generation

strengths: Unified framework for multiple crystal generation tasks (CSP, DNG, ATG) through clever decoupling of flow time axes, extending multimodal generative modeling to periodic systems
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two datasets (MP-20, MPTS-52) with extensive comparisons to recent strong baselines and thorough ablation studies validating design choices
Principled composition- and symmetry-aware atom ordering with quantified benefits (11 orders of magnitude permutation space reduction) and strong empirical motivation from crystallography
Practical advantages including faster inference saturation, novel atom type substitution capability, and consistent model scaling behavior across sizes
Detailed reproducibility information with hyperparameters, training configurations, inference algorithms, and honest limitations discussion including unresolved stability-novelty tradeoff
weaknesses: Mixed and modest performance improvements over baselines: MCFlow-B achieves 63.14% CSP match rate vs OMatG's 63.75% on MP-20; DNG shows lower novelty rates especially for larger models; lack of statistical significance testing (no error bars or confidence intervals)

Fundamental unresolved stability-novelty tradeoff (Table 2) where larger models generate more stable but less novel structures—a critical limitation for practical materials discovery that the paper acknowledges but does not address

Overstated claims about incorporating crystallographic symmetry 'without explicit templates' when Wyckoff positions used in ordering are explicit crystallographic information; misleading presentation of methodology

Limited core methodological novelty—decoupled time axes adapted from Multiflow, DiT backbone is prior work, flow matching is standard; contribution is primarily effective engineering/combination of existing techniques rather than fundamental innovation

Insufficient justification for design choices: why electronegativity ordering is optimal beyond empirical comparison, arbitrary-appearing loss weights (0.5/2.0/1.0/1.0), incomplete explanation of ordering ambiguity resolution during CSP inference when Wyckoff positions unknown

Incomplete computational cost analysis (per-step reported but not total wall-clock for comparable quality), only 4 examples for atom type substitution validation, missing comparison with recent concurrent work (Zatom-1)

strengths: Well-motivated multimodal framework using decoupled time variables (t,s) enabling flexible any-to-any modality generation in a single model
Thoughtful domain engineering with composition- and symmetry-aware atom ordering providing >11 orders of magnitude permutation space reduction
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three tasks (CSP, DNG, ATG) on multiple benchmarks with thorough ablations and reproducibility details
Strong empirical results on MPTS-52 and stability-related metrics in DNG, with superior space group distribution matching vs. baselines
Clean mathematical formulation with detailed algorithms and configurations enabling reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: primarily applies existing multimodal flow ideas (Multiflow, Rojas et al.) to crystals with domain-specific engineering rather than fundamental methodological advancement

Overstated symmetry claims: paper claims 'crystallographic symmetry learned from data without explicit templates' but explicitly uses Wyckoff positions (p.5, Algorithm 1), which encode space group information—distinction between 'soft' and 'hard' encoding is overstated
Modest improvements on standard MP-20 CSP benchmark: MCFlow-B achieves 63.14% vs. 63.75% for OMatG (slightly worse); atom ordering contributes ~2-3% (Table 5); noisy guidance adds ~1%

Unresolved stability-novelty trade-off (Table 2): larger models yield more stable but less novel samples—acknowledged but not analyzed or addressed, representing a fundamental limitation for a unified framework

Weak task motivation: structure-conditioned atom type generation (ATG) acknowledged as not previously studied as standalone task, raising questions about unification around unmotivated objectives; baseline uses property predictor (CGCNN) not generative model

Missing critical analysis: no explanation for why decoupling (t,s) is necessary (Table H.8 shows >17% degradation when coupled but reason unexplained); no analysis of what symmetries are actually learned or whether permutation augmentation enforces equivariance

Evaluation fairness concerns: excluding template-conditioned baselines for using 'structural templates' while MCFlow uses Wyckoff positions (crystallographic information) is inconsistent; template-conditioned comparison (Table H.3) shows MCFlow is competitive, not clearly superior
Limited scope: only inorganic crystals (MP-20, MPTS-52); no exploration of MOFs, proteins, or other domains; DNG stability depends on MLIP reliability without sensitivity analysis
Computational efficiency nuances: MCFlow-L is 3× larger but only ~1.5× faster/step than DiffCSP; training requires 2-4 days on single GPU

strengths: Novel unified multimodal flow framework with decoupled time axes enabling any-to-any modality generation across three distinct crystal generation tasks without retraining
Clever composition- and symmetry-aware atom ordering with hierarchical permutation augmentation providing >11 orders of magnitude permutation space reduction with principled theoretical justification
Comprehensive experimental evaluation on two benchmarks (MP-20, MPTS-52) with extensive ablations, multiple model scales, and standardized evaluation metrics (LeMat-GenBench)

Strong empirical results on MPTS-52 CSP (27.16% MR vs OMatG 25.15%) and superior symmetry distribution matching compared to FlowMM/ADiT, indicating capture of crystallographic constraints without explicit templates
Excellent reproducibility with detailed model/training/inference configurations, computational cost analysis, and clear presentation of methods and results
Geometrically stable generated samples (lower relaxation RMSE/steps, Figure 5) and faster integration step convergence (Figure 3) with practical efficiency gains
weaknesses: Critical ambiguity in Wyckoff position handling for CSP: paper lacks clear explanation of how Wyckoff positions are determined during structure generation when only composition is given, creating potential circular dependency that threatens method generality

Task-specific design choices (selective noisy guidance, manual loss weights, tuned NG parameters) undermine unified framework claim; Table H.7 shows unified training provides minimal benefit over CSP-only training (62.11% → 63.14%)

Incomplete CSP comparisons: template-conditioned baselines (DiffCSP++, SGFM) excluded from main results despite Table H.3 showing they outperform MCFlow under template conditioning; on MP-20, MCFlow-L only marginally improves OMatG (64.08% vs 63.75%)

Unresolved stability-novelty trade-off (Table 2): larger models generate fewer novel structures (18.6% vs 52.2%), suggesting bias toward known materials problematic for discovery, but lacks investigation of root causes or mitigation strategies

Incremental novelty in individual components: multimodal flow adapted from prior work, DiT is standard, noisy guidance from Rojas et al., ordering extends Cao et al.'s Wyckoff approach; main contribution is combination and application

Noisy guidance dependency for CSP (1% MR improvement) indicates core model limitations; sensitivity analysis (Figure E.1) shows brittleness at higher noise levels, suggesting post-hoc rather than fundamental improvement

Limited theoretical justification: why electronegativity ordering outperforms atomic number lacks deep analysis (Table H.4); mechanism by which permutation augmentation enables symmetry learning not clearly explained

Sparse error analysis: no systematic investigation of failure modes, only 4 examples for atom type substitution, no statistical significance testing, missing ablations on loss weight sensitivity and DNG/ATG response to decoupled time axes
